title: Cost of Debt
subtitle: The real after-tax interest rate on a loan
openingQuestion: A company borrows at 8%/year, tax rate 20%. What is the after-tax cost of debt?
explanation: The real cost of debt is lower than the interest rate written in the contract, because interest is deducted before tax is calculated: Kd after-tax = Kd × (1 − tax rate) = 8% × 0.8 = 6.4%. In other words, for every 100 units of interest owed, the government effectively covers 20 units through the reduced tax bill. This is the 'tax shield' - the reason debt is cheaper than equity, and also the reason a loss-making company (which pays no tax) loses this benefit entirely.

Interest is deducted before tax is calculated
Gives the after-tax cost of debt - lower than the stated rate

realWorldExample.description: When valuing a business, analysts typically look up the current yield to maturity (YTM) of that company's bonds trading in the secondary market - this is the most accurate way to estimate the current cost of debt, rather than using the rate on old loans signed years ago.

quiz.question: What's the most accurate way to estimate the cost of debt for a company with listed bonds?
options: Use the coupon rate printed on the bond at issuance
Use the interest rate on the most recent bank loan agreement
Use the YTM of the bond currently trading in the market
Use the interest expense divided by total outstanding debt on the books
quiz.explanation: The YTM of a listed bond reflects the real cost of raising new debt in the market today. An old contract rate doesn't reflect the current cost of borrowing.

quiz.question: Why can using the rate from a bank loan signed 5 years ago to calculate the current Cost of Debt give a misleading result?
options: Because banks usually reset the rate once a year
Because the old rate hasn't been adjusted for cumulative inflation
Because the old loan is nearly paid off so the balance is negligible
Because WACC needs the marginal cost of borrowing more right now
quiz.explanation: Cost of Debt in WACC should reflect the MARGINAL cost of borrowing - i.e. what the company would pay if it borrowed MORE right now - not the cost of historical loans locked in earlier, because WACC is used to evaluate FUTURE investment decisions.

quiz.question: Interest rate 9%, tax rate 20%. What is the after-tax cost of debt?
options: 7.2% (= 9% × 0.8, after the tax shield)
10.8% (= 9% × 1.2, adding the tax)
1.8% (= 9% × 20%, taking only the tax portion)
9% (tax has no effect on the cost of debt)
quiz.explanation: Kd after-tax = 9% × (1 − 0.2) = 7.2%. Every unit of interest paid reduces taxable income, so the government effectively covers this 1.8-percentage-point difference.

quiz.question: A company is losing money and pays no tax. What happens to the tax shield on its debt?
options: It stays the same because interest is always deductible regardless
It temporarily loses its effect, so the cost of debt equals the stated interest rate
It increases because the loss carries forward to future years
It can't be determined without knowing the exact size of the loss
quiz.explanation: With no taxable income, there's nothing to deduct against. This is one reason a loss-making company should be cautious with leverage: debt is both more expensive than it looks, and more dangerous.

quiz.question: A company's credit rating gets downgraded. What happens to its Cost of Debt?
options: Unchanged until the current loan matures
Falls, because the company needs to borrow to improve cash flow
Rises, because creditors demand a higher risk premium
Only rises if the company issues new bonds
quiz.explanation: A downgrade lowers the price of outstanding bonds, meaning YTM rises - and that is the company's new borrowing cost immediately, even before it borrows another dollar. WACC edges up accordingly.

keyTakeaways: After-tax Cost of Debt = Interest rate × (1 − Tax rate)
The tax shield makes debt cheaper than its stated rate
Use the YTM of current bonds, not the rate on old loan contracts

practicePrompt.question: A company borrows from a bank at an interest rate of 10%/year, with a corporate tax rate of 20%. What is the actual after-tax Cost of Debt on this loan, and why is it lower than the stated interest rate?
options: The after-tax Cost of Debt is 10% × (1 - 0.2) = 8%, because interest is deducted before tax is charged
Cost of Debt after-tax = 10% + 20% = 12%, adding the interest rate and the tax rate directly
Cost of Debt after-tax always equals the stated 10% because tax has no effect on the cost of debt
Cost of Debt after-tax = 10% × 20% = 2%, multiplying the interest rate directly by the tax rate
practicePrompt.explanation: Cost of Debt after-tax = Interest rate × (1 − Tax rate) = 10% × 0.8 = 8%. Because interest is deducted before corporate income tax is calculated, the tax saved (the tax shield) makes the real cost of debt lower than the stated rate - this is why debt is usually 'cheaper' than equity after tax adjustment.

summary.keyIdea: Cost of Debt after-tax = Interest rate × (1 − Tax rate)
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: The tax shield makes debt cheaper than its stated rate

application.title: Calculate the after-tax cost of debt
application.message: Take the interest rate on a loan (credit card, mortgage, or a corporate bond you follow) and multiply it by (1 − tax rate) to get the real after-tax cost of debt.
application.secondary: The gap between the stated rate and the after-tax cost is exactly the tax shield.

sections.text: Cost of Debt seems simple - just the interest rate on a loan - but there are two things to keep in mind: the real cost must be calculated after tax, and it's better to use the current market borrowing rate, not the rate on old loans signed years earlier.
The formula and the tax shield

Cost of Debt after-tax = Kd × (1 − Tax Rate). **Example:** a business borrows at 8%/year, corporate tax rate 20%: Kd after-tax = 8% × (1−0.2) = 8% × 0.8 = 6.4%. The real cost is lower than the stated interest rate because interest is deducted before corporate income tax is calculated - this tax savings is called the debt 'tax shield'.

The most accurate way to estimate Cost of Debt is to use the YTM (yield to maturity) of the company's bonds trading in the secondary market - because this reflects exactly what the company would pay if it borrowed more right now. Using the rate on a bank loan signed 5 years ago can be misleading, because credit conditions and market rates have changed since then - WACC needs to reflect the marginal cost of capital for future investment decisions, not a historical cost.

items: Kd after-tax = pre-tax Kd × (1 − tax rate)
The tax shield usually makes debt cheaper than equity on an after-tax cost basis
Prefer the YTM of current bonds over the rate on old loan contracts
A company without listed bonds can estimate this from its most recent bank borrowing rate or a comparable credit rating

lines: The fact that after-tax Cost of Debt is lower than the cost of equity is why businesses maintain a certain level of debt in their capital structure, rather than funding entirely with equity.
